newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Finland, Sweden stress Baltics' position in NATO enlargement.
newsitem.headline: Finland, Sweden stress Baltics' position in NATO enlargement.

text.p: Finland and Sweden stressed on Wednesday that the planned enlargement of the NATO military alliance must not take place in such a way that it worsens the security position of the three Baltic republics.
Reflecting the two countries' shared views on the issue, senior Finnish and Swedish foreign ministry officials met with NATO Assistant Secretary General Gebhard von Moltke in Brussels.
They also discussed the expanding cooperation between the two militarily non-aligned countries and the 16-nation North Atlantic Treaty Organisation, and other issues.

Jaakko Blomberg, Finnish under-secretary of state for political affairs, underlined the importance of the principle that enlargement does not take place in such a way that it "destabilises" those countries which may not be included in the first wave.

A NATO summit in July is expected to invite new membership applications. However, the Baltic republics of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania are not seen as likely to be in the first group of former communist countries to join NATO.

Ulf Hjertonsson, Swedish director-general for political affairs, said enlargement was especially sensitive in the northern part of Europe, stressing that each country must have the right to choose its own security arrangement.
"We are lobbying hard for the right of each European country to make its own security-policy choice," he told journalists after the meeting.
He noted that NATO itself had stressed that its enlargement must not create new divisions or spheres of interests in Europe.
An agreement between NATO and Russia must not take place at the expense of the interests of other countries, especially the Baltics, Hjertonsson said.

At their Helsinki summit this month, Russia and the United States agreed to disagree on NATO's expansion plans but vowed to press ahead with a charter to set a new relationship between Russia and NATO.
Finland and Sweden, which have no plans to seek NATO membership, share close historical and geographical ties with the three Baltics, which all want to join the alliance.
